title: Why Japan's Health Insurance Covers Herbal Medicine Without Modern Trials
hook: Nearly 150 traditional herbal formulas are prescribed by Japanese doctors and reimbursed by national insurance—most never passed a modern randomized trial.
target_query: why does japan's health insurance cover kampo herbal medicine
free_section_html:
Japan's national health insurance covers Kampo (kanpo, the Japanese adaptation of classical Chinese herbal medicine) because roughly 150 standardized formulas were added to the official drug price list in 1976, grandfathered in on the basis of centuries of recorded use rather than the double-blind randomized trials required of new pharmaceuticals today. Any physician with a normal medical license, not a specialist, can write a prescription for these products, and patients pay the same copayment—typically 30 percent—that they would for a blood pressure pill or an antibiotic.

The formulas are not loose herbal mixtures bought at a market stall. They are manufactured as standardized granules or extracts by licensed pharmaceutical companies under the same quality-control rules that apply to any other drug, and their prices are set through the government's periodic drug-pricing negotiations, the same process used for chemotherapy agents. One firm, Tsumura, has come to dominate this narrow but stable market, and by some industry estimates supplies the large majority of Kampo prescriptions written in Japanese hospitals.

The 1976 decision was less a scientific verdict than a political and administrative one. Kampo had survived a near-ban during the Meiji era's push toward Western biomedicine and clung on through small pharmacies and university medicine departments that kept detailed clinical records. When Japan's insurance bureaucracy, the Central Social Insurance Medical Council, expanded coverage lists in the 1970s, it accepted this accumulated clinical tradition as sufficient evidence for formulas already in wide use, without demanding they be re-tested against the emerging gold standard of the randomized controlled trial.

That arrangement has persisted for nearly five decades with only incremental change. New Kampo formulas proposed for insurance listing today do face modern trial requirements, but the original 1976 cohort was never retroactively re-examined at the same standard, creating two tiers of evidence sitting side by side on the same prescription pad. Understanding why that gap has survived, and what happens as Japan's aging population puts new pressure on drug spending, requires looking at how the system actually decides what stays covered.
paid_body_html:
The 1976 Decision That Changed Everything

Before the mid-1970s, Kampo occupied a marginal place in Japanese medicine. It had never been formally banned after the Meiji Restoration, but the government's decision in the late nineteenth century to license physicians only through Western-style medical education pushed herbal practice to the margins for nearly a century, kept alive mainly by pharmacists, a scattering of university departments, and family clinics that passed down formulas the way a craft is passed down. What changed was not a scientific breakthrough but a bureaucratic one. In 1976, Japan's Central Social Insurance Medical Council, known as Chuikyo, the body that decides which drugs and treatments the national health insurance system will pay for, added a batch of standardized Kampo extract granules to the official reimbursement list. The council accepted long clinical use, documented in classical texts and generations of case records, as the basis for coverage, rather than requiring the placebo-controlled trials that had already become standard for new Western pharmaceuticals entering the Japanese market around the same period.

The timing mattered. Japan had achieved universal health coverage in 1961, and by the 1970s the insurance system was mature enough, and politically confident enough, to make room for a domestic medical tradition that had strong support among practicing physicians and a manufacturing base ready to scale up production. Pharmaceutical companies that had been producing Kampo extracts on a small scale suddenly had a large, stable, insurance-backed market to sell into.

Two Tiers of Evidence on the Same Prescription Pad

The practical effect of the 1976 listing is that Japan now runs two evidentiary tracks for the same category of medicine. A newly proposed Kampo formula seeking insurance coverage today must go through modern clinical development, including controlled trials, much like any other drug. But the roughly 150 formulas grandfathered in during the 1970s were never required to clear that same bar retroactively. They remain listed, reimbursed, and prescribed on the strength of historical use and the clinical judgment accumulated since.

This is not unique to Japan in principle; many countries have older drugs on their formularies that predate current trial standards. What is distinctive is the scale and visibility of the arrangement in Japan, where herbal formulas sit openly alongside statins and antibiotics on the same insurance drug price list, prescribed by the same general physicians in the same consultation, with no requirement that the patient see a specialist or seek out an alternative medicine practitioner.

Where the Evidence Actually Stands

The scientific picture underneath this administrative arrangement is genuinely mixed, and Japanese researchers themselves have been active in trying to close the gap. Daikenchuto, a formula widely prescribed after abdominal surgery to help restore bowel movement, has been the subject of multiple Japanese clinical trials examining its effect on postoperative ileus, and is one of the better-studied Kampo formulas by modern standards, though results across trials have not been uniformly conclusive. Yokukansan, prescribed for behavioral and psychological symptoms of dementia such as agitation and irritability, has similarly drawn trial-based research interest, reflecting real demand from an aging population and the limited options available for these symptoms in any medical system.

Other widely dispensed formulas rest on much thinner modern evidence, supported mainly by decades of accumulated clinical experience and smaller observational studies rather than large controlled trials. Japanese medical societies have been candid, in professional literature and continuing education materials, that Kampo's evidence base is uneven across the roughly 150 covered formulas, and that this unevenness is a known, tolerated feature of the system rather than an oversight.

The Business Behind the Prescription Pad

Kampo's survival inside a heavily regulated insurance system also has a commercial dimension. A small number of manufacturers, with Tsumura widely regarded as the dominant player, produce the standardized granules and extracts that make up nearly all insurance-covered Kampo products in Japan. Because prices for these products are set through the same periodic government negotiations that govern all reimbursed drugs, manufacturers have had a strong incentive to keep formulas on the list rather than push for the kind of large-scale, expensive modern trials that might either confirm or overturn decades of clinical assumption. Physicians, for their part, have had little regulatory pressure to stop prescribing formulas that patients often request by name and that carry a low burden of documented serious side effects compared with many conventional drugs.

Pressure to Modernize

That equilibrium is now under quiet strain. Japan's health ministry faces mounting pressure to control drug spending as the population ages and the ratio of working taxpayers to retirees narrows, and periodic reviews of the insurance drug price list have begun to scrutinize lower-value prescriptions across the board, Kampo included. There has also been a slow but real increase in Japanese-led clinical research aimed at building modern evidence for individual formulas, partly to defend their place on the reimbursement list against future cost-cutting reviews, and partly because export ambitions for Kampo products in markets like the United States and Europe require exactly the kind of trial data that Japan's own system never demanded at home. The result is a system in transition: an herbal tradition that entered universal health insurance through the back door of historical trust now increasingly has to justify itself through the front door of the randomized trial, one formula at a time.
key_takeaways: Roughly 150 standardized Kampo formulas were added to Japan's national health insurance drug list in 1976 based on historical clinical use, not modern randomized trials.
Any general physician can prescribe insurance-covered Kampo products, and patients pay the same copayment as for conventional drugs.
New Kampo formulas seeking coverage today must undergo modern trial-based evaluation, creating two evidentiary tiers within the same drug category.
Some formulas, like daikenchuto for postoperative bowel recovery and yokukansan for dementia-related agitation, have real but mixed modern trial evidence behind them.
Rising healthcare costs from Japan's aging population are pushing regulators and manufacturers toward stronger evidence requirements for formulas that were grandfathered in decades ago.
